pharm: A dithiol (two sulfhydryl groups) chelator given by deep intramuscular injection in peanut oil; its thiol groups compete with tissue and enzyme sulfhydryl groups for arsenic, gold, mercury, and lead, forming stable metal-dimercaprol complexes that are excreted, protecting and reactivating thiol-dependent enzymes.
quick: Deep IM, dose by indication/severity (e.g. arsenic/gold mild 2.5 mg/kg QID then taper; severe 3 mg/kg q4h)
Use only in life-threatening poisoning; weigh risk vs benefit
Caution; use only if clearly needed
Renal impairment - use with great caution; the metal complex is renally excreted (can dissociate)
Discontinue if hepatic insufficiency arises during therapy (except postarsenical jaundice)
Avoid alcohol during therapy - can affect metal mobilization/excretion
BP, HR, fever (children), urine output/alkalinity, G6PD status (hemolysis); avoid in peanut allergy
summary: Dimercaprol (BAL, British Anti-Lewisite) is a dithiol heavy-metal chelating agent given by deep intramuscular injection in a peanut-oil/benzyl benzoate vehicle. It is indicated for arsenic, gold, and acute mercury poisoning, and as an adjunct (with calcium disodium EDTA) for acute lead poisoning, especially lead encephalopathy. Its two sulfhydryl groups bind metal ions to form a stable, excretable complex, sparing and reactivating thiol-dependent enzymes. Because the dimercaprol-metal complex can dissociate, especially in acid urine and renal impairment, the urine should be kept alkaline, and renal function watched. Common dose-related effects include hypertension with tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, headache, burning sensations, and (notably in children) fever. It can cause hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients, and the peanut-oil vehicle means it must be avoided in patients allergic to peanuts. It is contraindicated in hepatic insufficiency (except postarsenical jaundice) and in iron, cadmium, or selenium poisoning (toxic complexes).
indications: Acute mercury poisoning (if therapy begun within 1-2 hours of ingestion)
Acute lead poisoning, in combination with calcium disodium edetate (EDTA), particularly lead encephalopathy

dosage.d: 2.5 mg/kg four times daily for 2 days, then twice daily on the 3rd day, then once daily thereafter for 10 days
3 mg/kg every 4 hours for 2 days, then four times on the 3rd day, then twice daily thereafter for 10 days
Initial 5 mg/kg, then 2.5 mg/kg once or twice daily for 10 days
dosage.n: Most effective if started within 1-2 hours of ingestion; not effective for chronic mercury or organic mercury

dosage.d: 4 mg/kg alone for the first dose, then 4 mg/kg every 4 hours together with calcium disodium EDTA (given at a separate site)
dosage.n: Give dimercaprol first/with EDTA; ensure adequate urine flow before EDTA

dosage.d: 3 mg/kg every 4 hours combined with calcium disodium EDTA

admin: Administer by DEEP intramuscular injection only (it is formulated in peanut oil with benzyl benzoate)
Do NOT give to patients with peanut allergy because of the peanut-oil vehicle
Keep the urine alkaline to stabilize the dimercaprol-metal complex and protect the kidneys
When treating lead, give dimercaprol and calcium disodium EDTA at separate injection sites
Begin therapy as early as possible after exposure for best effect (especially mercury)
Ensure adequate hydration and urine output; monitor blood pressure and pulse around dosing
moa: Dimercaprol contains two free sulfhydryl (thiol) groups that have a high affinity for heavy-metal ions such as arsenic, gold, mercury, and lead. Toxic metals exert their effects largely by binding the sulfhydryl groups of essential cellular enzymes, inactivating them. Dimercaprol competes with these tissue thiols, binding the metal to form a relatively stable, water-soluble dimercaprol-metal complex (chelate) that is excreted in the urine and bile, thereby preventing or reversing the inhibition of sulfhydryl-dependent enzyme systems and allowing enzyme reactivation. Because the complex can dissociate, particularly in acidic urine, keeping the urine alkaline favors metal excretion and reduces renal redeposition.

absolute: Poisoning with iron, cadmium, or selenium (the dimercaprol-metal complex is more toxic than the metal alone, especially to the kidneys)
relative: Renal impairment (complex may dissociate; nephrotoxic) - use with extreme caution and monitor
monitor: Blood pressure and heart rate (dose-related hypertension/tachycardia)
Renal function and urine output, urine pH

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established. Dimercaprol should be used in pregnant women only in cases of life-threatening acute poisoning where the potential benefit clearly outweighs the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether dimercaprol is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised; use during breastfeeding only if clearly needed for serious poisoning.
renal: If renal insufficiency is present or develops during therapy, dimercaprol must be used with extreme caution, because the metal-dimercaprol complex is excreted by the kidney and may dissociate, redepositing metal and causing nephrotoxicity. Keep the urine alkaline to stabilize the complex, monitor renal function closely, and consider dialysis to remove the complex if acute renal failure occurs.
hepatic: Dimercaprol is contraindicated in hepatic insufficiency, with the exception of postarsenical jaundice. If hepatic insufficiency appears during therapy (and is not due to the arsenic itself), the drug should be discontinued.

major: Iron, cadmium, selenium - do NOT use dimercaprol; it forms toxic complexes, especially nephrotoxic ones (concurrent iron therapy should be withheld during dimercaprol treatment)
moderate: Medicinal iron supplements - withhold during dimercaprol therapy (toxic complex); restart after chelation
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol should be avoided during therapy as it may affect the disposition and excretion of mobilized metals.
interactions.diagnostics: Keep urine alkaline; monitor urinary metal excretion. May cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (check blood counts).

common: Rise in blood pressure with tachycardia
Burning sensation of the lips, mouth, throat and eyes
Feeling of constriction/pain in the chest
Pain or abscess at the injection site
serious: Nephrotoxicity (complex dissociation, especially with renal impairment or acid urine)
rare: Sterile or pyogenic abscess at injection site
emergency: Acute renal failure from metal-complex nephrotoxicity

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate before and after dosing (transient dose-related hypertension and tachycardia)
Body temperature, particularly in children (fever is common and may persist)
Renal function, urine output, and urine pH (keep urine alkaline)
Hemoglobin/hematocrit for hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients
Liver function (discontinue for new hepatic insufficiency unless postarsenical)
Serial blood/urine metal concentrations to guide therapy
counsel: This medicine is given as a deep injection into the muscle to remove poisonous metals from the body
The injection contains peanut oil - tell the team if you are allergic to peanuts
You may feel a burning in the mouth or throat, get a headache, feel nauseated, or have a brief rise in blood pressure - these usually pass
Children may run a fever during treatment; this is expected and will be watched
Drink fluids as advised; your urine will be checked and may be kept alkaline to protect the kidneys
Avoid alcohol during the course of treatment
pk: Metal binding begins soon after IM absorption (within 30-60 minutes)
Plasma peak about 30-60 minutes after deep IM injection
Short - distribution and metabolism/excretion largely complete within ~4 hours (hence frequent dosing)
Brief - frequent (e.g. every 4 h) dosing needed to maintain chelation
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light; oily injection
pearls: Heavy-metal chelator (BAL) for ARSENIC, GOLD, acute MERCURY, and (with EDTA) acute LEAD - especially lead encephalopathy
Given by DEEP IM only, in a PEANUT-OIL vehicle - contraindicated in peanut allergy
Causes HEMOLYSIS in G6PD deficiency - check G6PD status and watch hemoglobin
Do NOT use for iron, cadmium, or selenium poisoning - forms more toxic (nephrotoxic) complexes
Keep urine ALKALINE - the dimercaprol-metal complex dissociates in acid urine and can damage the kidneys; use cautiously in renal impairment
Dose-related hypertension with tachycardia and fever (children) are characteristic; withhold concurrent iron therapy
missed: Dimercaprol is administered by healthcare professionals on a fixed antidote schedule for acute poisoning; there is no self-administered dose to miss. If a scheduled dose is delayed, the treating team adjusts the regimen based on the poisoning severity and metal levels.
overdose: Overdose produces an exaggeration of the dose-related effects: severe hypertension and tachycardia, vomiting, convulsions, stupor, and coma; very high doses can cause death. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive - control blood pressure, manage seizures, support respiration, maintain hydration and renal function, and keep the urine alkaline. Most adverse reactions are transient because the drug is rapidly metabolized and excreted.
